title: Modern Physics I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Modern Physics curriculum bridging classical and quantum physics: special relativity and early quantum theory (blackbody radiation, photoelectric effect, Compton effect, Bohr model, de Broglie hypothesis, uncertainty principle), kept conceptual/semi-quantitative ahead of the rigorous 300L Quantum Mechanics sequence.

questions.question: The first postulate of Einstein's special theory of relativity states that:
options: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames
The speed of light depends on the motion of the observer
Time flows at the same rate for all observers regardless of motion
Mass is conserved independently of energy in all frames
questions.correct_answer: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial reference frames
questions.explanation: This is the principle of relativity: no inertial frame is preferred, and physical laws take the same form in all of them.

questions.question: The second postulate of special relativity states that:
options: The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer
The speed of light varies depending on the observer's velocity relative to the source
Only mechanical laws are invariant between inertial frames
Light requires a medium (ether) to propagate
questions.correct_answer: The speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer
questions.explanation: This postulate, confirmed by the Michelson-Morley experiment, asserts the constancy of the speed of light in vacuum (c) for all inertial observers.

questions.question: Time dilation refers to the phenomenon whereby:
options: A moving clock, as observed from a stationary frame, appears to run slower than an identical clock at rest
All clocks everywhere run at identical rates regardless of relative motion
Time moves backward for objects travelling faster than light
Clocks run faster the faster they move, without limit
questions.correct_answer: A moving clock, as observed from a stationary frame, appears to run slower than an identical clock at rest
questions.explanation: Time dilation is a direct consequence of special relativity: a clock moving relative to an observer is measured by that observer to tick more slowly than a clock at rest in their own frame.

questions.question: The time dilation formula relating proper time Δt₀ and dilated time Δt for an object moving at speed v is:
options: Δt = Δt₀ / √(1 − v²/c²)
Δt = Δt₀ × √(1 − v²/c²)
Δt = Δt₀ × (1 − v/c)
Δt = Δt₀ + v/c
questions.correct_answer: Δt = Δt₀ / √(1 − v²/c²)
questions.explanation: The dilated time interval measured in a frame where the clock is moving is the proper time divided by the Lorentz factor √(1 − v²/c²), which is always less than 1, making Δt > Δt₀.

questions.question: A spaceship travels at 0.8c relative to Earth. Approximately what is the Lorentz factor γ for this speed?
Length contraction refers to the phenomenon whereby:
options: An object's length, measured along its direction of motion by an observer at rest, appears shorter than its proper (rest-frame) length
All objects shrink uniformly in every direction as speed increases
Length increases as an object's speed increases
Length contraction applies only to light itself, not to material objects
questions.correct_answer: An object's length, measured along its direction of motion by an observer at rest, appears shorter than its proper (rest-frame) length
questions.explanation: Length contraction occurs only along the direction of relative motion; the contracted length L = L₀√(1 − v²/c²), where L₀ is the proper length measured in the object's own rest frame.

questions.question: A rod has a proper length of 10 m. When observed moving at a speed such that γ = 2, what is its measured (contracted) length?
options: 5 m
questions.correct_answer: 5 m
questions.explanation: L = L₀/γ = 10/2 = 5 m, since length contraction uses 1/γ = √(1 − v²/c²).

questions.question: According to special relativity, the relativistic mass (or momentum) of an object increases as its speed approaches:
options: The speed of light, c
Half the speed of light
Zero
It never changes regardless of speed
questions.correct_answer: The speed of light, c
questions.explanation: The relativistic momentum p = γm₀v grows without bound as v approaches c because the Lorentz factor γ diverges, which is why no massive object can be accelerated to reach c.

questions.question: The relativistic momentum of a particle of rest mass m₀ moving at speed v is given by:
options: p = γm₀v = m₀v/√(1 − v₂/c²)
p = m₀v (unchanged from classical mechanics)
p = m₀c²/v
p = m₀v²/c
questions.correct_answer: p = γm₀v = m₀v/√(1 − v₂/c²)
questions.explanation: Relativistic momentum modifies the classical formula by the Lorentz factor γ, ensuring momentum conservation holds in all inertial frames at relativistic speeds.

questions.question: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence relation is expressed as:
options: E = mc²
E = mc
E = m²c
E = mc³
questions.correct_answer: E = mc²
questions.explanation: This famous relation shows that mass and energy are equivalent and interconvertible, with c² (the speed of light squared) as the conversion factor.

questions.question: According to E = mc², if 1 gram of mass were completely converted into energy, approximately how much energy (in joules) would be released? (c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
options: 9 × 10¹³ J
questions.correct_answer: 9 × 10¹³ J

questions.question: In nuclear reactions such as fission and fusion, the immense energy released is a direct consequence of:
options: A small amount of mass being converted into energy according to E = mc²
Chemical bonds being broken and reformed
Frictional heating within the reactor
Simple kinetic energy transfer with no mass change
questions.correct_answer: A small amount of mass being converted into energy according to E = mc²
questions.explanation: The mass of the products in fission or fusion is slightly less than that of the reactants; this mass defect is converted into a large amount of energy via E = mc².

questions.question: In the relativistic (Einstein) velocity addition formula for two velocities u and v along the same direction, the combined velocity w is:
options: w = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²)
w = u + v
w = uv/c²
questions.correct_answer: w = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c²)
questions.explanation: Unlike classical (Galilean) velocity addition, the relativistic formula ensures that the combined velocity never exceeds c even when both u and v are close to c.

questions.question: A spaceship moving at 0.5c relative to Earth fires a probe forward at 0.5c relative to itself. What is the probe's speed relative to Earth, according to relativistic velocity addition?
questions.explanation: w = (0.5c + 0.5c)/(1 + (0.5c)(0.5c)/c²) = 1.0c/(1 + 0.25) = 1.0c/1.25 = 0.8c, illustrating that speeds never simply add to exceed c.

questions.question: Classical (Newtonian) physics failed to correctly predict the spectrum of blackbody radiation, a discrepancy famously known as:
options: The ultraviolet catastrophe
The photoelectric paradox
The Compton problem
The correspondence failure
questions.correct_answer: The ultraviolet catastrophe
questions.explanation: Classical theory (Rayleigh-Jeans law) predicted that radiated energy would increase without bound at short (ultraviolet) wavelengths, contradicting experimental observation, a failure termed the ultraviolet catastrophe.

questions.question: Planck resolved the blackbody radiation problem by proposing that:
options: Energy is emitted or absorbed by oscillators only in discrete packets (quanta), E = nhν
Light behaves purely as a continuous wave with no restriction on energy
All electromagnetic radiation has the same energy regardless of frequency
Blackbody radiation does not depend on temperature
questions.correct_answer: Energy is emitted or absorbed by oscillators only in discrete packets (quanta), E = nhν
questions.explanation: Planck's quantum hypothesis proposed that oscillators in a blackbody can only emit or absorb energy in discrete multiples of hν, which successfully matched the observed radiation spectrum.

questions.question: In Planck's quantum hypothesis, the energy of a single quantum of radiation is given by:
options: E = hν
E = h/ν
E = hλ
E = ν/h
questions.correct_answer: E = hν
questions.explanation: Here h is Planck's constant and ν is the frequency of the radiation; this simple but revolutionary relation underlies all of quantum theory.

questions.question: The photoelectric effect refers to the phenomenon in which:
options: Electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light of sufficiently high frequency shines on it
Light is completely absorbed by any metal regardless of frequency
Electrons are ejected from a metal only when very intense low-frequency light is used
A metal surface emits light when heated
questions.correct_answer: Electrons are ejected from a metal surface when light of sufficiently high frequency shines on it
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material surface upon absorption of electromagnetic radiation above a threshold frequency.

questions.question: Classical wave theory failed to explain the photoelectric effect because it predicted that:
options: Increasing light intensity alone (at any frequency) should eventually eject electrons, and there should be no threshold frequency
Only high-intensity red light could ever eject electrons
Electron ejection should occur instantaneously regardless of frequency, which matched experiment
No electrons could ever be ejected by light
questions.correct_answer: Increasing light intensity alone (at any frequency) should eventually eject electrons, and there should be no threshold frequency
questions.explanation: Classically, energy should accumulate over time regardless of frequency, so any frequency of sufficiently intense or prolonged light should eject electrons — contrary to the sharp threshold frequency actually observed.

questions.question: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that:
options: Light consists of discrete photons, each of energy hν, and an electron absorbs a single photon's energy at a time
Light is purely a continuous wave that gradually transfers energy to electrons
Electrons themselves carry quantized charge that determines emission
The metal surface vibrates at the frequency of incoming light
questions.correct_answer: Light consists of discrete photons, each of energy hν, and an electron absorbs a single photon's energy at a time
questions.explanation: Einstein extended Planck's quantum idea to light itself, proposing that light is quantized into photons; an electron is ejected only if a single photon's energy exceeds the metal's work function.

questions.question: Einstein's photoelectric equation relating the maximum kinetic energy KE_max of emitted electrons to the photon energy hν and the work function φ is:
options: KE_max = hν − φ
KE_max = hν + φ
KE_max = φ/hν
KE_max = hν × φ
questions.correct_answer: KE_max = hν − φ
questions.explanation: The maximum kinetic energy of an ejected photoelectron equals the incident photon's energy minus the work function (the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal).

questions.question: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. If light of photon energy 3.5 eV strikes the metal, what is the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons?
options: 1.5 eV
5.5 eV
2.0 eV
3.5 eV
questions.correct_answer: 1.5 eV
questions.explanation: KE_max = hν − φ = 3.5 eV − 2.0 eV = 1.5 eV.

questions.question: In the photoelectric effect, if the frequency of incident light is below the metal's threshold frequency, then:
options: No electrons are emitted, no matter how intense the light is
Electrons are still emitted but with reduced kinetic energy
Electrons are emitted only if the light is extremely intense
The metal begins to melt instead of emitting electrons
questions.correct_answer: No electrons are emitted, no matter how intense the light is
questions.explanation: Below the threshold frequency, each photon carries insufficient energy to overcome the work function, so no electrons are emitted regardless of the light's intensity, a key quantum prediction confirmed experimentally.

questions.question: The Compton effect refers to:
options: The increase in wavelength of X-rays (or gamma rays) scattered by a loosely bound electron, compared to the incident wavelength
The ejection of electrons from a metal by visible light
The emission of continuous radiation from a heated blackbody
The bending of light around a massive object
questions.correct_answer: The increase in wavelength of X-rays (or gamma rays) scattered by a loosely bound electron, compared to the incident wavelength
questions.explanation: Compton scattering demonstrates the particle nature of photons: a photon transfers some of its energy and momentum to a free (or loosely bound) electron, resulting in a scattered photon of longer wavelength (lower energy).

questions.question: The Compton effect provided strong evidence for which property of electromagnetic radiation?
options: That photons possess both energy and momentum, behaving as particles in collisions
That light is purely a wave with no particle-like behaviour
That electrons have no mass
That the speed of light varies with photon energy
questions.correct_answer: That photons possess both energy and momentum, behaving as particles in collisions
questions.explanation: By treating the photon-electron interaction as an elastic collision conserving both energy and momentum, Compton's analysis confirmed that photons carry momentum p = h/λ, reinforcing the particle nature of light.

questions.question: The Compton shift formula for the change in wavelength Δλ when a photon scatters off an electron through angle θ is:
options: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cosθ)
Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 + cosθ)
Δλ = (m_ec/h)(1 − cosθ)
Δλ = hν(1 − cosθ)
questions.correct_answer: Δλ = (h/m_ec)(1 − cosθ)
questions.explanation: This is the Compton scattering formula, where h/(m_ec) is the Compton wavelength of the electron (≈ 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m), and θ is the scattering angle of the photon.

questions.question: The Bohr model of the hydrogen atom postulates that electrons orbit the nucleus in:
options: Certain allowed (quantized) circular orbits without radiating energy
Any arbitrary orbit, continuously radiating energy as they move
Elliptical orbits identical to planetary motion with no quantization
A fixed single orbit regardless of the atom's energy state
questions.correct_answer: Certain allowed (quantized) circular orbits without radiating energy
questions.explanation: Bohr postulated that electrons occupy specific stationary states (quantized orbits) in which they do not radiate energy, resolving the classical problem of electrons spiralling into the nucleus.

questions.question: In the Bohr model, an electron emits a photon of radiation when it:
options: Transitions from a higher energy orbit to a lower energy orbit
Remains in the same stationary orbit indefinitely
Transitions from a lower energy orbit to a higher energy orbit
Moves in a straight line away from the nucleus
questions.correct_answer: Transitions from a higher energy orbit to a lower energy orbit
questions.explanation: A photon is emitted, with energy equal to the energy difference between the two orbits, when an electron drops from a higher to a lower allowed energy level.

questions.question: Bohr's quantization condition states that the angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is an integer multiple of:
options: h/2π (i.e., ħ)
h (Planck's constant itself)
2πh
h²
questions.correct_answer: h/2π (i.e., ħ)
questions.explanation: Bohr postulated that angular momentum L = nħ = nh/2π, where n is a positive integer (the principal quantum number), restricting electrons to specific discrete orbits.

questions.question: According to the Bohr model, the energy of the hydrogen atom in its n-th orbit is given by E_n = −13.6/n² eV. What is the energy of the ground state (n = 1)?
options: 0 eV
questions.explanation: Substituting n = 1 gives E₁ = −13.6/1² = −13.6 eV, the ground-state (lowest, most tightly bound) energy of the hydrogen atom.

questions.question: The discrete line spectra observed in hydrogen (e.g. the Balmer, Lyman, and Paschen series) are explained by the Bohr model as arising from:
options: Electron transitions between specific quantized energy levels, each transition emitting a photon of a specific wavelength
Continuous energy loss as electrons spiral inward towards the nucleus
Random thermal vibrations of the hydrogen nucleus
The Doppler effect due to atomic motion alone
questions.correct_answer: Electron transitions between specific quantized energy levels, each transition emitting a photon of a specific wavelength
questions.explanation: Each spectral line corresponds to a specific electron transition between two quantized energy levels, and since the allowed energies are discrete, only certain photon wavelengths (frequencies) are emitted or absorbed.

questions.question: The Lyman series in the hydrogen spectrum corresponds to electron transitions that end at which energy level?
options: n = infinity
questions.explanation: The Lyman series consists of transitions from higher energy levels down to the ground state (n = 1), producing spectral lines in the ultraviolet region.

questions.question: The de Broglie hypothesis proposes that:
options: Every moving particle has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p
Only photons have wave properties; matter particles are purely particle-like
Wavelength is independent of a particle's momentum
Large macroscopic objects show strong, easily observable wave behaviour
questions.correct_answer: Every moving particle has an associated wavelength given by λ = h/p
questions.explanation: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter, proposing that any particle with momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p, later confirmed experimentally (e.g. electron diffraction).

questions.question: Which experiment provided direct experimental confirmation of the de Broglie hypothesis for electrons?
options: The Davisson-Germer electron diffraction experiment
The Michelson-Morley experiment
Millikan's oil-drop experiment
Rutherford's gold foil scattering experiment
questions.correct_answer: The Davisson-Germer electron diffraction experiment
questions.explanation: Davisson and Germer observed diffraction patterns of electrons scattered from a nickel crystal, confirming that electrons exhibit wave-like behaviour consistent with de Broglie's predicted wavelength.

questions.question: An electron of momentum p = 2 × 10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s has a de Broglie wavelength of approximately (h ≈ 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s):
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = (6.63×10⁻³⁴)/(2×10⁻²⁴) ≈ 3.3×10⁻¹⁰ m, on the order of atomic dimensions.

questions.question: Wave-particle duality refers to the concept that:
options: Entities such as photons and electrons exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment
All particles are purely waves with no particle characteristics whatsoever
Waves and particles are entirely unrelated concepts in quantum theory
Only large macroscopic objects show dual wave-particle behaviour
questions.correct_answer: Entities such as photons and electrons exhibit both wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment
questions.explanation: Quantum entities display wave-like behaviour (e.g. interference, diffraction) in some experiments and particle-like behaviour (e.g. discrete collisions, localized detection) in others, and neither picture alone is complete.

questions.question: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that:
options: It is fundamentally impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle with arbitrary precision
Position and momentum can both be measured with unlimited precision simultaneously if instruments are good enough
Only energy and time are subject to any uncertainty relation
Uncertainty arises purely from limitations of measuring instruments, not from nature itself
questions.correct_answer: It is fundamentally impossible to simultaneously know both the exact position and exact momentum of a particle with arbitrary precision
questions.explanation: The uncertainty principle is a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics, not merely an experimental limitation — the product of the uncertainties in position and momentum has an inherent lower bound.

questions.question: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation for position (Δx) and momentum (Δp) is commonly expressed as:
options: Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2
Δx · Δp = 0
Δx + Δp ≥ h
Δx / Δp ≥ h
questions.correct_answer: Δx · Δp ≥ ħ/2
questions.explanation: This is the standard form of the position-momentum uncertainty relation, where ħ = h/2π, showing that the product of the uncertainties has a minimum non-zero value.

questions.question: A conceptual consequence of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is that:
options: The classical idea of a particle following a precisely defined trajectory (exact position and momentum simultaneously) breaks down at the quantum scale
Macroscopic objects like cars and footballs show easily observable positional uncertainty in everyday life
Energy can be created or destroyed without any physical consequence
Only photons, and no other particles, are subject to the uncertainty principle
questions.correct_answer: The classical idea of a particle following a precisely defined trajectory (exact position and momentum simultaneously) breaks down at the quantum scale
questions.explanation: Because Δx and Δp cannot both be arbitrarily small, quantum particles cannot be assigned a definite classical trajectory the way macroscopic objects can, though the effect is negligible for everyday-sized objects due to the smallness of ħ.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of observables also obeys an uncertainty relation analogous to position and momentum?
options: Energy and time
Charge and mass
Volume and pressure at constant temperature
Velocity and acceleration
questions.correct_answer: Energy and time
questions.explanation: An analogous uncertainty relation, ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2, links energy and time, meaning a state that exists for only a short time has a correspondingly large uncertainty in its energy.

questions.question: Which of these observations from classical physics's failures directly motivated the birth of quantum theory (as opposed to relativity)?
options: The inability of classical physics to explain the blackbody radiation spectrum and the photoelectric effect
The null result of the Michelson-Morley experiment
The precession of the perihelion of Mercury
The constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames
questions.correct_answer: The inability of classical physics to explain the blackbody radiation spectrum and the photoelectric effect
questions.explanation: The blackbody radiation problem and the photoelectric effect were key experimental puzzles that classical physics could not explain, directly motivating Planck's and Einstein's quantum hypotheses; the other options relate to the historical motivation for relativity, not quantum theory.

questions.question: At speeds much smaller than the speed of light (v << c), the relativistic formulas for time dilation, length contraction, and momentum reduce to:
options: The familiar classical (Newtonian) expressions
Formulas identical to the photoelectric equation
Zero for all quantities
Formulas that diverge to infinity
questions.correct_answer: The familiar classical (Newtonian) expressions
questions.explanation: This is the correspondence principle: relativistic mechanics reduces to Newtonian mechanics in the low-speed limit, since the Lorentz factor γ approaches 1 as v/c approaches 0.

questions.question: Two events that are simultaneous in one inertial reference frame are, in general:
options: Not simultaneous when observed from a different inertial frame moving relative to the first
Always simultaneous in every other inertial frame as well
Impossible to compare between different reference frames
Only non-simultaneous if the events occur at the same spatial location
questions.correct_answer: Not simultaneous when observed from a different inertial frame moving relative to the first
questions.explanation: The relativity of simultaneity is a key consequence of special relativity: whether two spatially separated events are simultaneous depends on the observer's reference frame.
